title: Software Supply Chain Compromise Affecting Clinical Application Vendors
summary: Compromise of a clinical software vendor's build and distribution infrastructure resulted in signed updates carrying attacker-added functionality being installed across downstream provider organisations.
content:
## Summary

This joint advisory is released to warn network defenders in the health and public health sector. Compromise of a clinical software vendor's build and distribution infrastructure resulted in signed updates carrying attacker-added functionality being installed across downstream provider organisations.

**Advisory type:** Cybersecurity Advisory

**Authoring agencies:** CISA, FBI, HHS

## Observed tactics, techniques and procedures

- Access to vendor build infrastructure through a compromised developer account
- Insertion of additional functionality prior to the code-signing step
- Distribution through the vendor's routine update channel to all customers
- Dormancy period before activation, exceeding typical log retention windows

## Recommended actions

- Require vendors to attest to build-pipeline controls, not only to secure development practices.
- Retain update-installation records beyond the typical dormancy period of this attack class.
- Baseline the outbound network behaviour of clinical applications so deviation is detectable.
- Include update-channel compromise explicitly in third-party risk assessments.

## Assessment

- A valid code signature attests to origin, not to integrity of intent, and cannot be relied on as a security control here.
- The dormancy period is chosen to exceed customer log retention, which is the decisive design feature of the attack.
- Detection realistically depends on behavioural baselining of the application, not on file reputation.
